The vocal-tract entry is the human-made model of the vocal tract as an acoustic filter cavity in speech production theory. It is defined entirely in terms of its role as the filter component in the source-filter model: the model decomposes speech into source (glottal-flow) and filter (vocal-tract), and the vocal-tract construct cannot be separated from this framework.

Pinned sense (Law 11d): videolaryngoscopy is laryngoscopy performed with the laryngeal image displayed on a video monitor — 'a camera at the tip of the scope replaces the direct line of sight' (its accepted definition). High-speed-videolaryngoscopy is that examination with a high-speed camera integrated into the laryngoscope recording the vocal folds at 2000-10000 fps: the camera-tipped scope and the recorded image field are exactly videolaryngoscopy's carve, with the added frame-rate parameter. A competent speaker would call HSV 'a videolaryngoscopy' (a high-speed one); videolaryngoscopy is the nearest accepted kind, closer than laryngoscopy itself, whose direct-vision carve is replaced by the camera. [Law 9, 11]

payload.name: glottal-insufficiency
payload.scope: People made glottal-insufficiency to categorize the failure of vocal fold closure during phonation or airway protection so that clinicians can identify the gap morphology, its etiology, and select appropriate treatment.

definition.body: Glottal insufficiency is a clinical construct that maps the failure of the vocal folds to achieve complete closure during phonation or airway protection, resulting in abnormal airflow and voice quality. Parameters: (1) the gap morphology - anterior commissure gap, posterior glottic chasm, unilateral or bilateral fold bowing, or asymmetric closure; (2) the etiology - vocal fold paralysis or paresis, presbylaryngis-related atrophy, sulcus vocalis, surgical resection, or neurologic degeneration; (3) the functional consequences - breathy voice quality, glottal airway leak measured by aerodynamic flow, compensatory hyperfunction of supraglottic structures, and potential aspiration risk. It persists as a maintained diagnostic category in laryngology classification systems, documented in clinical assessment protocols and surgical planning documents. e.g.: breathy voice with posterior glottic gap in a patient with unilateral vocal fold paralysis; bilateral bowing seen in presbylaryngis; complete glottic incompetence following bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury | not: glottic stenosis, which narrows the airway by scarring rather than failure of fold closure; laryngomalacia, which is supraglottic collapse rather than glottic closure failure [formal: insufficientia glottidis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.scope: People made laryngeal-motor-disorder to categorize neurological and mechanical failures of the laryngeal muscles that disrupt phonation and airway protection, enabling differential diagnosis and targeted intervention.

definition.body: Laryngeal motor disorder is a clinical construct that classifies conditions in which the neuromuscular control of the larynx is disrupted, producing abnormal voice, breathing, or swallowing. Parameters: (1) the motor pattern - hyperadductory, hypoadductory, or abductor failure; (2) the neurologic substrate - peripheral nerve injury (recurrent laryngeal nerve, superior laryngeal nerve), central nervous system lesion, peripheral neuropathy, or dystonic dysregulation; (3) the clinical phenotype - breathy voice from fold bowing, strained-strangled voice from spasm, breathiness on onset, or aspiration. It persists as a maintained classification in neurology and laryngology practice, documented in the Modified Neurologic Laryngology Scale and standardized assessment protocols. e.g.: adductor spasmodic dysphonia producing strained-strangled voice with glottic spasms; bilateral vocal fold paralysis from thyroid surgery damaging both recurrent laryngeal nerves; abductor spasmodic dysphonia causing inspiratory stridor | not: laryngeal-tumor, which is a structural mass lesion rather than a neuromuscular disorder; gastroesophageal-reflux, which causes laryngeal irritation without primary motor disruption [formal: disorder motorius laryngis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

definition.body: Presbylaryngis is a clinical construct that categorizes the progressive atrophy and tissue remodeling of the larynx associated with aging, producing characteristic voice and aerodynamic changes. Parameters: (1) the structural changes - atrophy of the vocalis muscle, thinning of the lamina propria layers, increased Reinke space compliance loss, calcification of thyroid and cricoid cartilages; (2) the aerodynamic consequence - reduced maximum phonation time, increased glottal airway leak, decreased subglottal pressure efficiency; (3) the acoustic phenotype - breathy voice with increased jitter and shimmer, reduced vocal range, decreased maximum intensity. It persists as a maintained diagnostic category in geriatric laryngology, documented in the Geriatric Voice Assessment Protocol and clinical text descriptions of age-related voice change. e.g.: breathy voice with glottic gap in an 80-year-old patient with bilateral vocal fold atrophy; reduced maximum phonation time to 8 seconds in presbylaryngis without other pathology; voice change documented over 5-year follow-up in a patient with progressive vocal fold bowing | not: presbycusis, which is age-related hearing loss affecting voice monitoring but not the laryngeal structures themselves; spasmodic dysphonia, which is a dystonic motor disorder rather than age-related atrophy [formal: presbylaryngis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: glottal-airway-leak
payload.scope: People made glottal-airway-leak as a measured construct quantifying the volume of air escaping through the glottis during phonation, enabling objective assessment of vocal fold closure efficiency.

definition.body: Glottal airway leak is a clinical measure that quantifies the volume of air escaping through the glottis during attempted phonation, reflecting the degree of vocal fold closure insufficiency. Parameters: (1) the measurement method - aerodynamic flow measured by pneumotachograph or digital voice analyzer during sustained vowel phonation; (2) the normalized metric - glottal airflow rate expressed in milliliters per second or as a percentage of total expiratory airflow; (3) the clinical threshold - normal closure (below 100 ml/s), mild leak (100-300 ml/s), moderate leak (300-600 ml/s), severe leak (above 600 ml/s). It persists as a maintained measurement standard in laryngology practice, documented in clinical voice assessment protocols and instrumental evaluation guidelines. e.g.: sustained /a/ phonation showing 450 ml/s glottal leak in a patient with unilateral vocal fold paralysis; normal glottal airflow of 40 ml/s in a healthy voice; elevated leak of 720 ml/s during bilateral vocal fold paralysis; pre- and post-injection comparison showing reduction from 500 ml/s to 80 ml/s after vocal fold augmentation | not: nasopharyngeal leak, which measures air escaping through the nose during oral speech; cough airflow, which is a protective reflex measurement not a phonatory assessment [formal: fugacium viae glottidis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: laryngeal-palpation
payload.scope: People made laryngeal-palpation to systematically assess the larynx through external hand contact, providing information about cartilage position, symmetry, and mobility that internal visualization cannot fully capture.

definition.body: Laryngeal palpation is a manual examination technique in which the clinician uses external finger pressure on the neck to assess the position, symmetry, mobility, and sensitivity of the laryngeal cartilages and surrounding structures. Parameters: (1) the palpation regions - thyrohyoid membrane, thyroid cartilage notch, cricothyroid space, cricoid cartilage, and the lateral soft tissues of the anterior neck; (2) the assessment targets - thyroid cartilage tilt and rotation, cricothyroid joint mobility, thyrohyoid distance change during phonation, subcutaneous emphysema, and tenderness or crepitus; (3) the clinical indications - suspected laryngeal trauma, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, laryngeal fracture, tracheoesophageal speech assessment, or preoperative airway evaluation. It persists as a maintained clinical skill in laryngology and otolaryngology training, documented in physical examination textbooks and clinical practice guidelines. e.g.: palpating the thyrohyoid membrane for increased tension during vowel phonation; assessing cricothyroid joint mobility by lateral finger pressure on the cricothyroid space; palpating the neck for crepitus following laryngeal trauma; subcutaneous emphysema on laryngeal palpation after laryngeal surgery [formal: palpatio laryngea | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: vocal-fold-augmentation
payload.scope: People made vocal-fold-augmentation to map the injectable materials and techniques used to medialize paralyzed or atrophic vocal folds, enabling comparison of biomaterials and clinical outcomes.

definition.body: Vocal fold augmentation is a clinical construct that categorizes injectable biomaterials and the procedural techniques used to increase the bulk of atrophic or paralyzed vocal folds, improving glottic closure and voice quality. Parameters: (1) the injectable material - autologous fat, calcium hydroxylapatite, carboxymethylcellulose gel, polytetrafluoroethylene paste, hyaluronic acid, or collagen; (2) the procedural route - percutaneous transthyroid injection under local or general anesthesia, direct laryngoscopic injection under microlaryngoscopy, or endoscopic injection with laryngeal nerve guidance; (3) the duration of effect - temporary (absorbed in weeks to months), intermediate (6-12 months), or permanent (fibrosis or integration). It persists as a maintained procedural category in phonosurgical practice, documented in the Voice Enhancement Consensus Statement and standardized laryngeal surgery textbooks. e.g.: percutaneous injection of calcium hydroxylapatite (Restylane) for unilateral vocal fold paralysis; fat graft medialization for presbylaryngis-related vocal fold atrophy; autologous fat augmentation in a patient with bilateral vocal fold atrophy following thyroid cancer resection | not: thyroplasty type I, which is a cartilage window implant rather than an injectable augmentation; botulinum-toxin-injection, which reduces muscle activity rather than adding bulk [formal: augmentatio plicae vocalis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

The laryngeal-motor-disorder construct classifies neuromuscular failures of the larynx producing abnormal voice; glottal-insufficiency is the hypoadductory subtype where the motor pattern is inadequate adduction. payload.name: vocal-fold-closure-efficiency
payload.scope: People made vocal-fold-closure-efficiency to quantify the completeness of vocal fold apposition during phonation, providing a numeric basis for assessing glottal competence.

definition.body: Vocal-fold-closure-efficiency is a quantitative metric that expresses the proportion of glottal closure achieved during phonation, derived from aerodynamic or imaging measures of airflow and contact area. Parameters: (1) measurement modality - aerodynamic flow, electroglottography contact quotient, or high-speed video contact area; (2) normalization - ratio of measured closure to maximal achievable closure under the same subglottal pressure; (3) reporting units - percentage or dimensionless ratio. It persists as a maintained analytic construct in voice research and clinical voice assessment, documented in peer-reviewed methods and software toolkits. e.g.: 85% closure efficiency measured by electroglottography in normal phonation; 40% efficiency in unilateral vocal fold paralysis measured by aerodynamic flow; high-speed video showing 92% contact area in trained singers | not: vocal fold mobility, which assesses movement rather than closure completeness; fundamental frequency, which measures pitch rather than closure [formal: efficientia clausurae plicae vocalis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: clinical-assessment-of-voice
payload.scope: People made clinical-assessment-of-voice to standardize perceptual voice quality rating through a structured 9-point scale, providing a replicable perceptual anchor that complements acoustic and aerodynamic measures in voice-disorder assessment.

definition.body: Clinical-assessment-of-voice (CAPEV) is a standardized perceptual protocol for rating overall voice quality on a 9-point categorical scale, developed to provide a replicable perceptual anchor for voice-disorder severity. Parameters: (1) the scale — a 9-point ordinal scale ranging from 'normal' (0) through increasing degrees of dysphonia to 'severely dysphonic' (8), with standardized verbal descriptors for each point; (2) the rating procedure — a trained listener (speech-language pathologist, audiologist, or laryngologist) rates a voice sample (sustained vowel, connected speech, and/or speech samples) based on global severity; (3) the reliability protocol — multiple raters, typically 3–5 trained listeners, provide independent ratings averaged for final severity score. Persistence mechanism: the standardized perceptual protocol documented in voice assessment literature, implemented in clinical voice evaluation workflows, maintained by the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association and the Voice Society, and used as a clinical standard in voice-disorder research and practice. e.g.: the CAPEV protocol as described in Stemple et al.'s Clinical Voice Assessment; CAPEV severity rating performed by three trained SLPs on dysphonic patient samples; CAPEV scale used alongside AVQ and GRBAS in a laryngeal muscle-tension dysphonia study; CAPEV rating of sustained /a/ in a Mayo Clinic voice laboratory validation study | not: GRBAS, which uses separate dimension ratings rather than a single global severity scale [formal: aestimatio vocis clinicalis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: mean-flow-rate
payload.scope: People made mean-flow-rate to quantify the average aerodynamic airflow through the glottis during phonation, providing a simple ratio measure of respiratory support relative to vocal-fold efficiency in sustained phonation.

definition.body: Mean-flow-rate is an aerodynamic measure quantifying the average airflow through the glottis during sustained phonation, computed as the ratio of exhaled volume to phonation duration. Parameters: (1) the vital capacity measurement — the total exhaled volume during the maximal phonation task, measured by spirometry; (2) the phonation duration — the total time of voiced production from the maximum phonation time measurement; (3) the computation — mean flow rate = vital capacity / maximum phonation time, typically reported in ml/s or L/s. It persists as a maintained clinical parameter in voice assessment protocols, documented in laryngology textbooks, implemented in aerodynamic measurement systems, and taught in speech-language pathology curricula as a standard screen for respiratory support efficiency. e.g.: mean-flow-rate of 145 ml/s calculated from 2900 ml VC divided by 20 s MPT in a healthy adult; mean-flow-rate of 95 ml/s in bilateral vocal fold paralysis; mean-flow-rate of 200 ml/s in a trained singer with high vital capacity | not: glottal airflow waveform g(n), which is the per-frame time series, not an aggregate ratio; peak glottal flow, which measures the instantaneous maximum within a cycle rather than the sustained average [formal: fluxus medius | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: nasalance-score
payload.scope: People made nasalance-score to quantify the proportion of acoustic energy radiated through the nose during oral speech production, providing an objective measure of velopharyngeal competence for hypernasality assessment.

definition.body: Nasalance-score is an aerodynamic measure quantifying the ratio of acoustic energy radiated through the nasal port to total acoustic energy during speech, expressed as a percentage. Parameters: (1) the nasal microphone — captures acoustic energy radiated through the nostrils; (2) the oral microphone — captures acoustic energy radiated from the lips; (3) the nasalance computation — percentage = 100 * nasal_mic_energy / (nasal_mic_energy + oral_mic_energy); (4) the speech stimuli — a set of oral-dominant words (e.g., 'happy,' 'puppy') and nasal-dominant words (e.g., 'mummy,' 'bunny') that establish baseline oral and nasal nasalance values. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical protocol documented in speech-language pathology literature, implemented in NASOMETER equipment by Kay PENTAX, used in clinical voice and speech assessment, and maintained as a standard measure of velopharyngeal function. e.g.: NASOMETER oral nasalance of 12% measured in a typical speaker reading oral words; nasalance of 55% measured in a patient with cleft palate and velopharyngeal insufficiency; baseline nasal nasalance of 72% established on nasal words in a speech assessment protocol | not: GRBAS rating of breathiness, which is a perceptual dimension not an aerodynamic measurement; nasopharyngoscopy, which directly visualizes velopharyngeal closure rather than measuring acoustic output [formal: gradus nasalis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.scope: A human-authored acoustic measure designed to quantify amplitude perturbation in voiced speech by computing the decibel difference between the first harmonic and the noise floor in a short-time spectrum, then converting that difference to a logarithmic quotient.

definition.body: Normalized amplitude quotient (NAQ, also NQI) is an acoustic parameter quantifying the relative amplitude of the fundamental harmonic to the noise floor in a short-time spectrum of voiced speech. Computed as NAQ = log10(10^(H1/20) - 1), where H1 is the amplitude difference in dB between the first harmonic peak and the mean noise floor at the same fundamental frequency. Parameters: (1) the fundamental frequency F0 from pitch tracking to locate the first harmonic, (2) the spectral analysis frame (window type, length, and resolution), (3) the noise floor estimation method (mean power spectral density in non-harmonic bins). A higher NAQ indicates greater harmonic-to-noise separation (clearer phonation); lower NAQ indicates increased noise relative to the fundamental (breathy or dysphonic voice). Persistence mechanism: implemented as a standard parameter in acoustic voice analysis toolkits including Praat (via the VoiceStat plugin), VoiceSauce, and laryngology assessment software; documented in peer-reviewed voice-quality literature. e.g.: NAQ computed from a 200-ms sustained /a/ segment in a laryngology clinic intake using Praat VoiceStat; NAQ reported as a component of the acoustic voice-quality index in a muscle-tension dysphonia study; NAQ threshold value of 1.56 used to differentiate typical from disordered phonation in a pediatric voice assessment [formal: quotientia amplitudinis normalisatae | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: voice-therapy
payload.scope: People made voice-therapy to retrain a patient's voice production through structured therapeutic methods, so that voice disorders whose presentations arise from maladaptive phonation behavior, muscle tension, or post-surgical laryngeal dysfunction can be treated without surgery.

definition.body: Voice-therapy is a human-authored therapeutic scheme for reshaping voice production: a maintained family of structured methods that retrains a patient's phonation - breath support, laryngeal posture, resonance, and fold adduction - to treat voice disorders whose presentations arise from maladaptive phonation behavior, muscle tension, or post-surgical or post-paralytic laryngeal dysfunction. It is the maintained map of the territory of treatable voice disorders: what is treated, by which method, and by whom. Parameters: (1) the method families - resonant voice therapy, semi-overt articulation, vocal function exercises, and the Mead-Voice program for spasmodic dysphonia, each with a documented protocol; (2) the patient indications - functional (muscle-tension) dysphonia, vocal hyperfunction, post-surgical voice care, spasmodic dysphonia; (3) the delivery protocol - perceptual and instrumental assessment, a treatment goal tied to the mechanism, structured practice, and re-assessment; (4) the practitioner role - a speech-language pathologist or laryngologist trained in the method. It persists as a maintained practice: documented in voice-therapy textbooks and the Journal of Voice literature, delivered in laryngology and speech-language clinics, trained in graduate SLP and laryngology programs, and revised as methods are compared in clinical studies. e.g.: resonant voice therapy (RVT) protocol for functional hoarseness as published in the Journal of Voice; the Lee-Liban Vocal Function Exercises method for hyperfunctional dysphonia; the semi-overt articulation (SOV) method for muscle-tension dysphonia; the Mead-Voice therapy program for spasmodic dysphonia | not: injection laryngoplasty (a surgical treatment of the larynx, not therapeutic retraining); vocal rest (a prescription of reduced use, not a structured method); speech therapy for articulation disorders (treating a different territory) [formal: curatio vocis | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: medialization-thyroplasty
payload.scope: People made medialization-thyroplasty to restore glottic closure in a patient whose vocal fold no longer adducts, by implanting a medializing prosthesis through a thyroid window, so that the voice, airway, and swallow are restored without removing the larynx.

definition.body: Medialization thyroplasty is a laryngeal surgical technique that restores glottic closure by implanting a prosthesis that pushes the vocal fold medially. It is performed through a window in the thyroid lamina, created after a horizontal incision and retraction of the strap muscles, with the implant positioned between the window and the fold's lamina propria so the paralyzed or atrophic fold is carried toward the midline during phonation. Parameters: (1) the type - Type I, medializing a paralyzed, atrophic, or retracted fold to close a glottic gap, and Type III, reducing the upper airway space in hyperfunction; (2) the window - its position on the thyroid lamina, its dimensions, and the approach (open or endoscopic); (3) the implant - its material (silicone, hydroxyapatite, Gore-Tex, or autologous tissue), size, and shape; (4) the intraoperative setting - the degree of medialization adjusted under laryngoscopic inspection during phonation. It persists as a maintained surgical technique: documented in laryngology and otolaryngology textbooks and the voice-surgery literature, performed in laryngology clinics and voice-surgery centers, taught in laryngology training and fellowship programs, and revised as implant materials and endoscopic approaches improve. e.g.: a Type I thyroplasty with a silicone implant closing a glottic gap in unilateral vocal fold paresis; a Type III thyroplasty in hyperfunctional dysphonia with laryngoglottic insufficiency; an endoscopic medialization thyroplasty with a Gore-Tex implant for a persistent glottic gap after nerve resection | not: injection laryngoplasty (a percutaneous injection with no thyroid window); cricothyroid approximation (a different surgical route to glottic closure); laser excision of a vocal-fold mass (reductive surgery, not medialization) [formal: thyroplastia medializans | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

It is performed through a window in the thyroid lamina, created after a horizontal incision and retraction of the strap muscles, with the implant positioned between the window and the fold's lamina propria so the paralyzed or atrophic fold is carried toward the midline during phonation. Parameters: (1) the type - Type I, medializing a paralyzed, atrophic, or retracted fold to close a glottic gap, and Type III, reducing the upper airway space in hyperfunction; (2) the window - its position on the thyroid lamina, its dimensions, and the approach (open or endoscopic); (3) the implant - its material (silicone, hydroxyapatite, Gore-Tex, or autologous tissue), size, and shape; (4) the intraoperative setting - the degree of medialization adjusted under laryngoscopic inspection during phonation. It persists as a maintained surgical technique: documented in laryngology and otolaryngology textbooks and the voice-surgery literature, performed in laryngology clinics and voice-surgery centers, taught in laryngology training and fellowship programs, and revised as implant materials and endoscopic approaches improve. e.g.: a Type I thyroplasty with a silicone implant closing a glottic gap in unilateral vocal fold paresis; a Type III thyroplasty in hyperfunctional dysphonia with laryngoglottic insufficiency; an endoscopic medialization thyroplasty with a Gore-Tex implant for a persistent glottic gap after nerve resection | not: injection laryngoplasty (a percutaneous injection with no thyroid window); cricothyroid approximation (a different surgical route to glottic closure); laser excision of a vocal-fold mass (reductive surgery, not medialization) [formal: thyroplastia medializans | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: injection-laryngoplasty
payload.scope: People made injection-laryngoplasty to restore glottic closure in a patient whose vocal fold no longer adducts, by injecting a viscoelastic filler medial to the vocal fold through a percutaneous or endoscopic route, so that voice, airway, and swallow are restored without a thyroid window or laryngectomy.

definition.body: Injection laryngoplasty is a laryngeal surgical technique that restores glottic closure by injecting a viscoelastic filler medial to the vocal fold, so the paralyzed or atrophic fold is carried toward the midline during phonation. It is performed percutaneously through the thyroarytenoid membrane under direct laryngoscopic guidance, or transorally through an endoscopic route, with the needle advanced into the lamina propria of the fold and the filler deposited in the fold's midline while the degree of closure is adjusted during phonation on the laryngoscope. Parameters: (1) the access route - percutaneous needle injection under laryngoscopic control, or transoral endoscopic injection; (2) the filler material and its viscosity and duration - hyaluronic acid, calcium hydroxylapatite, collagen, or autologous fat, each with a documented resorption and duration profile; (3) the injection volume and placement - the fold's lamina propria or, for hyperfunction, the false fold; (4) the intraoperative setting - the closure assessed by laryngoscopic observation during phonation before the needle is withdrawn. It persists as a maintained surgical technique: documented in laryngology and otolaryngology textbooks and the voice-surgery literature, performed in laryngology clinics and voice-surgery centers, taught in laryngology training and fellowship programs, and revised as new filler materials and endoscopic routes are compared in clinical studies. e.g.: a percutaneous hyaluronic-acid injection laryngoplasty for unilateral vocal fold paralysis; a calcium-hydroxylapatite (Radiesse) injection for glottic insufficiency after unilateral paresis; an autologous fat injection laryngoplasty for a persistent glottic gap | not: medialization-thyroplasty (a window-based implant, not a percutaneous injection); thermal vocal-fold coagulation (a destructive procedure, not a filler injection); injection for a vocal-fold cyst (a lesion treatment, not glottic closure) [formal: laryngoplastia per injectionem | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

definition.body: Speech-language pathology is the clinical discipline of communication and swallowing: the assessment, diagnosis, and treatment of disorders of speech sounds, voice, language, fluency, cognition-communication, and swallowing, by examination and therapeutic intervention. Parameters: (1) the disorder territories - speech sound disorders, voice disorders, language disorders, fluency disorders, cognitive-communication disorders, and dysphagia; (2) the examination methods - standardized tests, perceptual evaluation, and instrumental assessment of articulation, prosody, and swallowing, with laryngeal structure referred to laryngology; (3) the treatment methods - articulation and resonance retraining, voice therapy, language therapy, fluency shaping, and swallowing therapy, each a structured protocol of goal, practice, and re-assessment; (4) the practitioner role - a licensed speech-language pathologist, certified through graduate training. It persists as a maintained discipline: licensed and certified through professional bodies, practiced in hospitals, schools, and private clinics, documented in its journals, and revised as evidence accumulates. e.g.: the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association's scope of practice and certification standards; a speech-language pathologist delivering resonant voice therapy for muscle-tension dysphonia; a speech-language pathologist providing swallowing therapy for a post-stroke dysphagia patient | not: laryngology (which examines and treats the larynx by direct visualization and surgery, not by communicative retraining) [formal: pathologia sermonis et deglutionis | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: recurrent-laryngeal-nerve
payload.scope: People made recurrent-laryngeal-nerve to identify and map the branch of the vagus nerve that innervates the intrinsic muscles of the larynx, so that laryngeal innervation and nerve injury can be diagnosed and managed in voice and airway disorders.

definition.body: Recurrent laryngeal nerve is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the branch of cranial nerve X (vagus) that supplies motor innervation to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid, and provides sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa below the vocal folds. Parameters: (1) the anatomical course — left nerve loops under the aortic arch, right nerve under the subclavian artery; (2) the motor targets — posterior cricoarytenoid, lateral cricoarytenoid, transverse and oblique arytenoids, thyroarytenoid, vocalis; (3) the sensory territory — laryngeal mucosa inferior to the vocal fold level; (4) the clinical relevance — left nerve injury more common due to longer course and proximity to thyroid and mediastinal structures. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark: mapped in Gray's Anatomy and Netter's Atlas, assessed via laryngeal electromyography, and referenced in surgical anatomy for thyroidectomy and laryngology. e.g.: Gray's Anatomy description of the recurrent laryngeal nerve's course from the vagus to laryngeal entry; Netter's Atlas plate showing the nerve's relationship to the inferior thyroid artery; laryngeal EMG needle recording from posterior cricoarytenoid muscle during nerve stimulation | not: superior-laryngeal-nerve (innervates cricothyroid and supraglottic mucosa, not intrinsic laryngeal muscles); vagus-nerve (cranial nerve X, the parent nerve of which RLN is one branch) [formal: nervus laryngeus recurrens | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: vocal-fold-nodules
payload.scope: People made vocal-fold-nodules to classify and name the bilateral symmetrical lesions of the vocal fold mucosa caused by chronic phonotrauma, so that clinicians can diagnose, stage, and manage this common voice disorder with standardized terminology.

definition.body: Vocal fold nodules are the human-authored anatomical-diagnostic construct identifying bilateral, symmetrical, benign lesions of the vocal fold free edge caused by chronic phonotrauma. Parameters: (1) the location — typically at the junction of anterior one-third and posterior two-thirds of the vocal folds (point of maximum vibration amplitude); (2) the histology — epithelial thickening, basement membrane disruption, and fibrovascular core; (3) the etiology — repetitive mechanical stress from excessive voice use, poor phonation technique, or vocal abuse; (4) the demographic — more common in children and female voice users, but occurs across populations. It persists as a maintained diagnostic category: classified in ICD-10-CM as J18.9 with specification, documented in laryngology textbooks (Koufman, Rosen), assessed via videostroboscopy, and managed through voice therapy or phonomicrosurgery. e.g.: ICD-10-CM classification of bilateral vocal fold nodules (J18.9 with specification); videostroboscopic image showing symmetric bilateral nodules at anterior-posterior junction; Rosen's Phonomicrosurgery textbook description of nodulectomy procedure | not: vocal fold cyst (unilateral lesion with distinct histology and location); polyp (unilateral, asymmetric lesion with different etiology) [formal: noduli cordis vocalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: phonotrauma
payload.scope: People made phonotrauma to name and classify the spectrum of laryngeal tissue injury caused by mechanical stress from voice use, so that clinicians can link voice behavior to pathology and design targeted prevention and treatment.

definition.body: Phonotrauma is the human-authored diagnostic concept mapping the spectrum of laryngeal tissue damage caused by excessive or abusive mechanical stress during phonation. Parameters: (1) the mechanism — repetitive impact forces between vocal folds exceeding tissue healing capacity during the open phase; (2) the dose-response — cumulative effect of frequency, intensity, and duration of voice use relative to vocal fold resilience; (3) the tissue response — from transient edema (vocal fatigue) through hemorrhage to epithelial hyperplasia and fibrosis; (4) the behavioral correlates — vocal abuse (screaming, yelling), vocal misuse (improper technique, excessive laryngeal tension), and vocal overuse (prolonged use beyond physiological limits). It persists as a maintained concept in laryngology and speech-language pathology: referenced in voice disorder pathophysiology textbooks (Hirano, Titze), used in patient education and voice hygiene protocols, and cited in etiological classifications of voice disorders. e.g.: Hirano's Basic Acoustics, Phoniatrics, and Phonopathology description of phonotrauma mechanisms; vocal hemorrhage following sustained yelling documented in a singer's medical record; ASHA clinical practice guidelines for voice hygiene and phonotrauma prevention | not: vocal-fold-hemorrhage (a specific acute injury event, not the conceptual category of injury); vocal-fatigue (a transient functional state, not structural tissue damage) [formal: phonotrauma | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: laryngeal-paralysis
payload.scope: People made laryngeal-paralysis to name and localize the loss of vocal-fold movement from laryngeal nerve injury, so that laryngology and otolaryngology can diagnose the cause of breathy voice and glottic gap and choose among observation, reinnervation, and medialization surgery.

definition.body: Laryngeal-paralysis is the human-authored diagnostic concept mapping the loss of vocal-fold movement caused by laryngeal nerve injury, classifying natural presentations by the nerve injured and the resulting position of the fold. Parameters: (1) the innervation it identifies - recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, in which the paralyzed posterior cricoarytenoid leaves the fold resting in a paramedian or abducted position, versus superior laryngeal nerve injury, in which cricothyroid paresis narrows the pitch range; (2) the classification maintained by the discipline - unilateral versus bilateral involvement, adducted versus abducted position of the affected fold, complete paralysis versus partial paresis; (3) the assessment it organizes - videostroboscopic observation of fold mobility, nasendoscopic examination, and laryngeal electromyography that dates the onset of denervation; (4) the etiologies it maps - iatrogenic injury from thyroid or cervical surgery and endotracheal intubation, tumor invasion, and idiopathic post-infectious palsy. It persists as a maintained diagnostic category in laryngology and otolaryngology: classified in ICD-10-CM (R13.1, paralysis of larynx), documented in laryngology textbooks and clinical examination reports, taught in otolaryngology curricula, and revised as reinnervation and medialization treatment evolve. e.g.: the diagnosis of unilateral vocal-fold paralysis documented in a laryngology consultation after total thyroidectomy; the ICD-10-CM code R13.1 (Paralysis of larynx) assigned in a hospital discharge record; the classification of a paralyzed fold into adducted versus abducted position in a videostroboscopic examination report; laryngeal electromyography used in a neurology consultation to date the onset of a recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy | not: the recurrent laryngeal nerve (the anatomical structure whose injury causes the presentations the category maps); dysphonia (the presentation the category names as one organic mechanism, not itself a mechanism category) [formal: paralysis laryngis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: laryngeal-electromyography
payload.scope: People made laryngeal-electromyography to read the electrical activity of the laryngeal muscles with needle electrodes, so that laryngology and speech-language pathology can distinguish active denervation from reinnervation, date a laryngeal-nerve injury, and choose between observation and surgical intervention.

definition.body: Laryngeal-electromyography is the clinical electrophysiological technique that records the electrical activity of the laryngeal muscles with needle electrodes, distinguishing active denervation from reinnervation in laryngeal-nerve injury. Parameters: (1) the target muscles - posterior cricoarytenoid and thyroarytenoid (recurrent laryngeal nerve territory) and cricothyroid (superior laryngeal nerve territory); (2) the signals recorded - motor unit potentials with their morphology and firing pattern, fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves of active denervation, and reinnervation changes; (3) the classification maintained by the discipline - active denervation versus reinnervation, and acute versus chronic injury staging that guides whether recovery is expected; (4) the practice in which it persists - needle placement during awake examination, recording in the laryngeal muscle, and reading the potentials against the established pattern of denervation and reinnervation, taught in laryngology, otolaryngology, and speech-language pathology training and documented in laryngological examination reports. e.g.: needle EMG of the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle in a laryngology clinic; the ASHA Clinical Practice Guideline on laryngeal electromyography; fibrillation potentials read as active denervation in a laryngeal examination report | not: a surface-EMG recording of the neck during speech; a nerve conduction study of the vagus [formal: electromyographia laryngea | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

Parameters: (1) the target muscles - posterior cricoarytenoid and thyroarytenoid (recurrent laryngeal nerve territory) and cricothyroid (superior laryngeal nerve territory); (2) the signals recorded - motor unit potentials with their morphology and firing pattern, fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves of active denervation, and reinnervation changes; (3) the classification maintained by the discipline - active denervation versus reinnervation, and acute versus chronic injury staging that guides whether recovery is expected; (4) the practice in which it persists - needle placement during awake examination, recording in the laryngeal muscle, and reading the potentials against the established pattern of denervation and reinnervation, taught in laryngology, otolaryngology, and speech-language pathology training and documented in laryngological examination reports. e.g.: needle EMG of the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle in a laryngology clinic; the ASHA Clinical Practice Guideline on laryngeal electromyography; fibrillation potentials read as active denervation in a laryngeal examination report | not: a surface-EMG recording of the neck during speech; a nerve conduction study of the vagus [formal: electromyographia laryngea | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: phonosurgery
payload.scope: People made phonosurgery to group the surgical operations on the larynx that are performed to treat voice and airway disorders, so that laryngology and otolaryngology can name, refer for, and plan these procedures under one discipline rather than by their individual operations.

definition.body: Phonosurgery is the human-authored discipline-map grouping the surgical operations on the larynx that are performed to treat voice and airway disorders, organized by the glottic problem the operation corrects. Parameters: (1) the operation families it groups - resection of lesions (nodulectomy, polypectomy, cordectomy), restoration of glottic closure (medialization thyroplasty, injection laryngoplasty, arytenoid adduction, thyroarytenoidization), and alteration of the framework (cricothyroidotomy, framework reconstruction); (2) the classification it maintains - operations grouped by their target, the glottic gap or the vocal-fold mass, which is the laryngological distinction between closure-restoring and lesion-removing surgery; (3) the practice in which it persists - taught in laryngology and otolaryngology surgical training, documented in the operative reports of laryngeal surgery, and maintained in the referral and planning language of the discipline. e.g.: medialization thyroplasty performed as phonosurgery to close a glottic gap from vocal-fold paralysis; injection laryngoplasty performed as phonosurgery for glottic insufficiency; nodulectomy performed as phonosurgery to remove bilateral vocal-fold nodules; arytenoid adduction performed as phonosurgery for a bilateral-abducted glottic gap | not: a laryngoscopy (the examination that precedes the operation, not the operation); a thyroidectomy (the operation on the thyroid gland, adjacent territory, not on the larynx for voice) [formal: chirurgia phoniatrica | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: spasmodic-dysphonia
payload.scope: People made spasmodic-dysphonia to name and distinguish the involuntary spasms of the laryngeal muscles that disrupt voice production, so that laryngology and speech-language pathology can diagnose it, tell dystonic spasms apart from voluntary muscle tension, and treat it with its specific methods.

definition.body: Spasmodic-dysphonia is the human-authored diagnostic concept mapping the involuntary spasms of the laryngeal muscles that disrupt voice production, classifying natural presentations by the muscle that spasms and the resulting voice quality. Parameters: (1) the spasm patterns it identifies - adductor spasms of the thyroarytenoid and interarytenoid muscles producing a strained-strangled quality, versus abductor spasms of the posterior cricoarytenoid producing an intermittent breathy break, the discipline's central distinction; (2) the clinical profile it maintains - adult-onset voice disorder, more common in women, dystonic in character, often with a family history, and not explained by voluntary muscle tension or a structural lesion; (3) the assessment it organizes - laryngoscopy and stroboscopy showing the spasm pattern, and laryngeal electromyography that distinguishes adductor from abductor involvement; (4) the treatment it maps - laryngeal botulinum toxin injection as the standard intervention and the Mead-Voice program as the behavioral therapy, the two disciplines' named treatments of this category. It persists as a maintained diagnostic category in laryngology and speech-language pathology: classified in ICD-10-CM (R49.0 with specification), documented in laryngology and voice-therapy literature, and revised as botulinum and behavioral treatments evolve. e.g.: the diagnosis of adductor spasmodic dysphonia in a laryngology consultation report; the Mead-Voice therapy program applied to a spasmodic-dysphonia patient; the classification of adductor versus abductor spasmodic dysphonia in the laryngology literature | not: muscle-tension dysphonia (the voluntary laryngeal hyperfunction the category is distinguished from); the thyroarytenoid muscle (the muscle that spasms, not the category of its spasms) [formal: dysphonia spasmodica | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: vocal-fold-cyst
payload.scope: People made vocal-fold-cyst to classify and name the unilateral benign lesions of the vocal fold mucosa caused by duct obstruction or trauma, so that clinicians can diagnose, stage, and manage this distinct voice pathology with standardized terminology.

definition.body: Vocal-fold-cyst is the human-authored anatomical-diagnostic construct identifying unilateral, benign lesions of the vocal fold mucosa caused by duct obstruction or localized trauma, distinct from phonotraumatic lesions. Parameters: (1) the cyst types - retention cysts arising from obstructed mucous glands in the superficial lamina propria, inclusion cysts from trapped squamous epithelium, and serous cysts from obstructed serous glands; (2) the location - typically on the free edge of the vocal fold at any point along its length, without the strict anterior-posterior junction predilection of nodules; (3) the histology - epithelial-lined cavity containing mucoid, serous, or keratinous material, surrounded by compressed normal lamina propria; (4) the clinical presentation - hoarseness, reduced pitch range, vocal fatigue, and often a unilateral stiffening of the vocal fold visible on stroboscopy. definition.body: Vocal-fold-hemorrhage is the human-authored diagnostic concept mapping the acute hemorrhage into the vocal fold mucosa that occurs when traumatic voice use ruptures subepithelial blood vessels. definition.body: Laryngeal-denervation is the human-authored diagnostic concept mapping the loss of motor nerve supply to the intrinsic laryngeal muscles, classifying denervation by the affected nerve branch and its resulting functional deficit. Parameters: (1) the nerve territories - recurrent laryngeal nerve (innervating all intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid, causing the affected fold to rest in paramedian position) and superior laryngeal nerve (innervating cricothyroid only, causing pitch range narrowing and voice fatigue); (2) the staging - acute denervation with fibrillation potentials on laryngeal EMG, early reinnervation with polyphasic motor unit potentials, and chronic denervation with permanent paralysis and fibrosis; (3) the etiologies - thyroid surgery (most common iatrogenic cause), endotracheal intubation, cervical trauma, tumor invasion, and post-infectious neuritis; (4) the functional assessment - videostroboscopic mobility grading, acoustic measures (jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio), and laryngeal EMG for denervation/reinnervation classification. definition.body: The supraglottis is the human-authored anatomical construct that maps the region of the larynx above the vocal folds, bounded inferiorly by the level of the vocal fold tips and superiorly by the epiglottis and hyoepiglottic ligament, whose function is airway protection during swallowing and resonance modification. Parameters: (1) the structures it includes - the epiglottis (leaflet that folds to cover the glottis during swallowing), the aryepiglottic folds (mucosal folds connecting arytenoid cartilages to epiglottis), the false vocal folds (ventricular folds above the true vocal folds), and the laryngeal ventricles (spaces between false and true vocal folds); (2) the protective function - the supraglottic closure sequence during swallowing (epiglottic inversion, aryepiglottic fold adduction, false vocal fold compression) that prevents aspiration; (3) the pathological territory - supraglottic cancer (epiglottic carcinoma, aryepiglottic fold tumors), supraglottitis (acute inflammatory swelling), and laryngocele (air-filled dilation of the laryngeal ventricle). It persists as a standard anatomical region in human anatomy texts, TNM cancer staging systems, and laryngological classification, providing the structural referent for airway protection research and supraglottic surgery. e.g.: the supraglottis as defined in Gray's Anatomy; the TNM staging system for supraglottic carcinoma by the AJCC; endoscopic view of aryepiglottic fold adduction during swallowing | not: the epiglottis alone (the supraglottis is a region, not a single structure); the subglottis (the region below the vocal folds) [formal: supr glottis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The subglottis is the human-authored anatomical construct that maps the region of the larynx below the vocal folds and above the tracheal rings, whose primary function is conducting inspired air from the glottis to the lower airway. Parameters: (1) the boundaries - superiorly defined by the inferior margin of the vocal folds extending to the inferior margins of the cricoid cartilage (approximately 1 cm below the glottis), inferiorly continuous with the first tracheal ring; (2) the structural characteristics - the subglottic mucosa is thin and firmly adherent to the underlying cricoid cartilage, making it the narrowest portion of the pediatric airway and the most susceptible site for subglottic stenosis; (3) the blood supply - the anterior subglottis receives dual blood supply from superior thyroid arteries (above) and inferior thyroid arteries (below), forming a watershed zone critical to surgical planning; (4) the pathological territory - subglottic stenosis (post-intubation or idiopathic), subglottic hemangioma (infantile vascular tumor), and subglottic squamous cell carcinoma. definition.body: The subglottis is the human-authored anatomical construct that maps the region of the larynx below the vocal folds and above the tracheal rings, whose primary function is conducting inspired air from the glottis to the lower airway. Parameters: (1) the boundaries - superiorly defined by the inferior margin of the vocal folds extending to the inferior margins of the cricoid cartilage (approximately 1 cm below the glottis), inferiorly continuous with the first tracheal ring; (2) the structural characteristics - the subglottic mucosa is thin and firmly adherent to the underlying cricoid cartilage, making it the narrowest portion of the pediatric airway and the most susceptible site for subglottic stenosis; (3) the blood supply - the anterior subglottis receives dual blood supply from superior thyroid arteries (above) and inferior thyroid arteries (below), forming a watershed zone critical to surgical planning; (4) the pathological territory - subglottic stenosis (post-intubation or idiopathic), subglottic hemangioma (infantile vascular tumor), and subglottic squamous cell carcinoma. It persists as a standard anatomical region in human anatomy texts, airway management guidelines, and laryngological classification, providing the structural referent for airway surgery and intubation safety. e.g.: the subglottis as defined in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; the Pediatric Advanced Life Support airway size chart referencing subglottic diameter; the ICD-10-CM code J38.4 (Stenosis of larynx) assigned for subglottic stenosis | not: the trachea (the region below the subglottis with complete cartilaginous rings); the cricoid cartilage (the supporting structure, not the anatomical region itself) [formal: subglottis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: vocal-process
payload.scope: People made the vocal-process construct to identify the posterior attachment point of the vocal fold on the arytenoid cartilage, so that clinicians can locate its anatomical landmarks for surgery, biopsy, and procedural planning.

definition.body: The vocal process is the human-made anatomical landmark identifying the triangular projection on the superior aspect of the arytenoid cartilage's lamina where the vocalis muscle inserts anteriorly and the vocal fold attaches posterolaterally. Parameters: (1) the geometry - a triangular projection approximately 4-6 mm long extending anterolaterally from the arytenoid lamina, providing the posterior anchor point for the vocal fold; (2) the attachments - the vocalis muscle inserts on the anteromedial surface, the vocal fold ligament and mucosa attach to the lateral margin, and the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle inserts on the posterolateral surface; (3) the clinical significance - the most posterior point of the vocal fold and the site of granulation tissue formation in intubation-related injury, the target for botulinum toxin injection in adductor spasmodic dysphonia, and the surgical landmark for arytenoid repositioning; (4) the surgical relationships - the vocal process lies at the junction of the subglottis (anterior) and supraglottis (lateral/superior), with the interarytenoid muscle crossing the midline posteriorly. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in laryngology atlases, surgical anatomy texts, and procedural guidelines. e.g.: the vocal process as depicted in Langman's Medical Anatomy; the surgical landmark for arytenoidectomy described in Rosen's Phonomicrosurgery textbook; the injection target point for botulinum toxin at the vocal process documented in voice therapy protocols | not: the arytenoid cartilage (the entire cartilage of which the process is a part); the vocal fold (the mucosal band attached to the process, not the bony projection itself) [formal: processus vocalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: glottis
payload.scope: People made the glottis construct to map the space between the vocal folds whose periodic opening and closing modulates airflow during phonation and respiration, so that clinicians can assess airway patency, voice production, and glottal pathologies.

definition.body: The glottis is the human-authored anatomical construct that maps the space between the two vocal folds and the intervening posterior mucosal area, whose open-close cycle modulates airflow from the lungs into the supraglottis during phonation and respiration. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — laterally bounded by the vocal processes of the arytenoid cartilages, anteriorly by the free edges of the true vocal folds, and posteriorly by the mucosal bridge connecting the arytenoids; (2) the functional states — abducted (widely open for breathing), adducted (closed for phonation and airway protection), and the intermediate vibratory state where periodic opening and closing generates the glottal airflow waveform; (3) the aerodynamic role — subglottal air pressure builds against the adducted folds until Bernoulli forces and tissue elasticity drive oscillation, producing the glottal source signal. It persists as a standard anatomical region in human anatomy texts, laryngology classification systems, and airway management guidelines, providing the structural referent for all phonation biomechanics and voice pathology assessment. e.g.: the glottis as defined in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; the glottal airflow waveform measured by nasendoscopy during sustained /a/ phonation; the glottal opening area during whispered phonation shown in high-speed videoendoscopy | not: the vocal folds themselves (the tissues that border the glottis but are not the space); the larynx (the entire organ that contains the glottis) [formal: glottis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: arytenoid-cartilage
payload.scope: People made the arytenoid cartilage construct to identify the paired pyramidal cartilage on which the vocal folds attach and from which the intrinsic laryngeal muscles act, so that clinicians can locate this critical landmark for airway management and laryngeal surgery.

definition.body: The arytenoid cartilage is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the paired pyramidal cartilages sitting atop the cricoid cartilage at the posterior aspect of the larynx, whose vocal and muscular processes serve as attachment and lever points for the vocal folds and intrinsic laryngeal muscles. Parameters: (1) the geometry — a pyramidal shape with a base resting on the cricoid articular surface, an apex topped by the corniculate cartilage, and three surfaces (anterior, medial, lateral); (2) the vocal process — an anterior projection from which the vocal ligament and mucosa extend laterally to form the posterior anchor of the vocal fold; (3) the muscular process — a lateral projection serving as the insertion point for the posterior cricoarytenoid (abductor) and lateral cricoarytenoid (adductor) muscles; (4) the articular facet — the concave base articulating with the cricoid cartilage to permit rotation and sliding motions that open and close the glottis. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology atlases, and surgical anatomy, providing the structural referent for all procedures involving vocal fold mobility and laryngeal framework surgery. e.g.: the arytenoid cartilages as illustrated in Gray's Anatomy, 51st edition; the cricoarytenoid joint motion demonstrated during videostroboscopy; arytenoid repositioning for unilateral vocal fold paralysis per Rosen's Laryngeal Framework Surgery | not: the cricoid cartilage (the complete ring-shaped cartilage below the arytenoids); the corniculate cartilage (the small nodule sitting on each arytenoid apex, a separate ossicle) [formal: cartilago arytenoidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: superior-laryngeal-nerve
payload.scope: People made the superior laryngeal nerve construct to identify the branch of the vagus nerve that divides into internal sensory and external motor divisions serving the upper larynx, so that surgeons can avoid injury during thyroidectomy and clinicians can assess upper laryngeal function.

definition.body: The superior laryngeal nerve is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the branch of cranial nerve X (vagus) that arises at the inferior vagal ganglion and divides into two terminal branches: the internal laryngeal nerve providing sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds, and the external laryngeal nerve providing motor innervation to the cricothyroid muscle. Parameters: (1) the course — descends on the pharyngeal constrictor, the internal branch pierces the thyrohyoid membrane alongside the superior laryngeal artery; (2) the internal laryngeal division — sensory to the supraglottic larynx including the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, and false vocal folds, with the afferent fibers contributing to the cough reflex; (3) the external laryngeal division — descends on the inferior pharyngeal constrictor to innervate the cricothyroid muscle, which tenses and elongates the vocal fold for high-pitch phonation; (4) the clinical relevance — external branch injury produces voice fatigue and pitch instability, assessed by measuring maximum phonation time and frequency range. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark: mapped in surgical anatomy texts, preserved via vessel-tie technique in thyroidectomy. e.g.: the superior laryngeal nerve anatomy shown in Gray's Anatomy 51st edition; the external branch identified during high-tie thyroidectomy per Carnavit's technique; maximum phonation time testing to detect subtle cricothyroid dysfunction | not: the recurrent-laryngeal-nerve (innervates all other intrinsic laryngeal muscles; courses differently); the vagus-nerve (the parent nerve from which SLN branches at the nodose ganglion) [formal: nervus laryngeus superior | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cricothyroid-muscle
payload.scope: People made the cricothyroid muscle construct to identify the laryngeal muscle that tenses and elongates the vocal folds via the cricothyroid joint, so that clinicians can assess its function in pitch production and surgical planning for voice disorders.

definition.body: The cricothyroid muscle is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the paired muscle forming the anterolateral wall of the larynx between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, whose contraction tilts the thyroid cartilage forward relative to the cricoid, thereby tensing and elongating the vocal folds to raise pitch. Parameters: (1) the origins — anteriorly the cricothyroid ligament and the anterior arch of the cricoid cartilage; (2) the insertion — the inferior margin and inferior horn of the thyroid cartilage; (3) the action — tilts the thyroid cartilage downward and forward on the cricoid articular facets, increasing the distance between the thyroid cartilage and vocal processes, which stretches and tenses the vocal folds; (4) the innervation — exclusively by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, making it uniquely susceptible to isolated denervation injury; (5) the functional role — the primary pitch-raising muscle, activated in high-frequency phonation, emotional vocalizations, and protective airway closure. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts and laryngology, providing the structural referent for cricothyroidotomy airway procedures and cricoarytenoidectomy surgery. e.g.: the cricothyroid muscle dissection shown in Gray's Anatomy 51st edition; the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve stimulation during thyroidectomy; cricothyroidotomy (emergency surgical airway through the cricothyroid membrane) per ATLS guidelines | not: the thyroarytenoid muscle (runs within the vocal fold and relaxes it, innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve); the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle (the only vocal fold abductor, innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve) [formal: musculus cricothyroideus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: vagus-nerve
payload.scope: People made the vagus nerve construct to identify the tenth cranial nerve that provides parasympathetic and motor innervation to the larynx and other thoracoabdominal viscera, so that clinicians can diagnose and manage laryngeal neuropathies and autonomic disorders.

definition.body: The vagus nerve is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the tenth cranial nerve (CN X), the longest cranial nerve that carries motor, sensory, and parasympathetic fibers from the medulla oblongata through the neck, thorax, and abdomen to the gastrointestinal tract. Parameters: (1) the cranial course — emerges from the medulla, exits the skull via the jugular foramen alongside the glossopharyngeal and accessory nerves; (2) the superior laryngeal branch — divides at the inferior vagal ganglion into internal laryngeal (sensory) and external laryngeal (motor) divisions; (3) the recurrent laryngeal branches — the right nerve hooks under the right subclavian artery, the left under the aortic arch, both ascending in the tracheoesophageal groove; (4) the parasympathetic distribution — provides vagal efferents to the heart, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract; (5) the sensory distribution — carries general sensation from the larynx, pharynx, ear, and viscera. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in neuroanatomy texts, surgical anatomy, and clinical neurophysiology, providing the structural referent for vagus nerve stimulation therapy and cranial nerve assessment. e.g.: the vagus nerve course shown in Gray's Anatomy 51st edition; the vagus nerve stimulation electrode placement for epilepsy per NIH guidelines; jugular foramen syndrome demonstrating CN X palsy with CN IX and XI deficits | not: the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX, exits the skull at the same jugular foramen but is separate); the accessory nerve (CN XI, travels alongside the vagus but supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius) [formal: nervus vagus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: posterior-cricoarytenoid-muscle
payload.scope: People made the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle construct to identify the sole abductor of the vocal folds, so that clinicians can assess its role in airway protection and its vulnerability to recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.

definition.body: The posterior cricoarytenoid muscle is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the paired laryngeal muscle originating on the posterior surface of the cricoid cartilage and inserting on the muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage, whose contraction abducts (opens) the vocal folds by rotating the arytenoids. Parameters: (1) the origin — the posterior surface and lateral margin of the cricoid cartilage; (2) the insertion — the muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage; (3) the action — pulls the muscular process posteriorly, rotating the arytenoid so the vocal process moves laterally, thereby abducting the vocal fold and opening the glottis; (4) the innervation — exclusively by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, making it dependent on RLN integrity; (5) the clinical significance — complete RLN injury paralyzes both PCA muscles, leaving the vocal folds in a paramedian position and causing severe dyspnea. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, laryngology atlases, and airway management guidelines, providing the structural referent for all procedures involving vocal fold paralysis and airway rescue. e.g.: the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle dissection shown in Gray's Anatomy 51st edition; bilateral vocal fold paralysis managed with tracheostomy when PCA function is lost; electromyographic denervation of the PCA in recurrent laryngeal nerve injury | not: the lateral cricoarytenoid muscle (adductor closing the glottis, same nerve but opposite action); the thyroarytenoid muscle (runs within the vocal fold wall, relaxing it) [formal: musculus cricoarytoideus posticus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: thyroarytenoid-muscle
payload.scope: People made the thyroarytenoid muscle construct to identify the intrinsic laryngeal muscle that runs within the vocal fold wall and relaxes the vocal fold by shortening it, so that clinicians can assess its role in phonation and its innervation by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

definition.body: The thyroarytenoid muscle is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the paired intrinsic laryngeal muscle extending from the thyroid cartilage anteriorly to the arytenoid cartilage posteriorly, whose contraction shortens and relaxes the vocal folds to lower pitch. Parameters: (1) the origin — the inner surface of the thyroid cartilage at the angle, just below the thyroid notch; (2) the insertion — the anterior surface and lateral margin of the arytenoid cartilage, with fibers interweaving with the vocalis muscle; (3) the vocalis muscle — the deep medial fibers of the thyroarytenoid that run parallel to the vocal fold ligament, fine-tuning vocal fold tension independently of gross arytenoid rotation; (4) the action — shortens the distance between the thyroid cartilage and arytenoid, relaxing the vocal folds and decreasing tension; (5) the functional role — the primary voice relaxer, active in low-pitch phonation, and the structural substrate within which the vocal fold ligament lies. definition.body: The thyroarytenoid muscle is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the paired intrinsic laryngeal muscle extending from the thyroid cartilage anteriorly to the arytenoid cartilage posteriorly, whose contraction shortens and relaxes the vocal folds to lower pitch. Parameters: (1) the origin — the inner surface of the thyroid cartilage at the angle, just below the thyroid notch; (2) the insertion — the anterior surface and lateral margin of the arytenoid cartilage, with fibers interweaving with the vocalis muscle; (3) the vocalis muscle — the deep medial fibers of the thyroarytenoid that run parallel to the vocal fold ligament, fine-tuning vocal fold tension independently of gross arytenoid rotation; (4) the action — shortens the distance between the thyroid cartilage and arytenoid, relaxing the vocal folds and decreasing tension; (5) the functional role — the primary voice relaxer, active in low-pitch phonation, and the structural substrate within which the vocal fold ligament lies. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts and laryngology, providing the structural referent for vocal fold medialization procedures and intramuscular botulinum toxin injections. e.g.: the thyroarytenoid muscle cross-section shown in Gray's Anatomy 51st edition; vocal fold medialization injection laryngoplasty targeting the vocalis muscle; intramuscular botulinum toxin injection for adductor spasmodic dysphonia at the thyroarytenoid per Benninger's protocol | not: the cricothyroid muscle (tenses vocal fold, opposite action, innervated by superior laryngeal nerve); the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle (abducts the fold, not within the fold wall) [formal: musculus thyroarytenoideus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: vocal-fold-polyp
payload.scope: People made the vocal-fold-polyp construct to classify the unilateral benign growths of the vocal fold mucosa that arise from focal mechanical trauma or chronic irritation, so that clinicians can distinguish them from bilateral symmetric lesions and apply the correct treatment.

definition.body: The vocal fold polyp is the human-authored anatomical-diagnostic construct identifying unilateral, benign growths of the vocal fold mucosa that arise from focal mechanical trauma or chronic irritation, distinct from bilateral symmetric lesions. Parameters: (1) the types — sessile polyps arising from subepithelial hemorrhage or fibrosis, pedunculated polyps on a stalk projecting from the vocal fold edge, and diffuse polyps extending beyond the free edge; (2) the location — typically on the free edge of the vocal fold, often at the junction of anterior one-third and posterior two-thirds, but without the strict bilateral symmetry of nodules; (3) the histology — fibrovascular stroma with varying degrees of vascular proliferation, mucoid degeneration, or epithelial hyperplasia; (4) the clinical presentation — persistent hoarseness, dysphonia, voice fatigue, and reduced pitch range on direct laryngoscopy showing a unilateral protrusion of the vocal fold edge. It persists as a maintained diagnostic category: classified in ICD-10-CM (J38.1), documented in laryngology textbooks (Koufman, Rosen, Cummings), assessed via videostroboscopy, and managed through phonomicrosurgical excision or voice therapy. e.g.: ICD-10-CM code J38.1 assigned for a unilateral vocal fold polyp in a surgical operative report; videostroboscopic image of a pedunculated polyp on the left vocal fold free edge; Rosen's Phonomicrosurgery textbook description of polypectomy technique; Koufman's Clinical Voice Disorders textbook case of a sessile hemorrhagic polyp | not: vocal fold nodules; vocal fold cyst [formal: polypus cordis vocalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]
